objectives.text: Identify major pharmacologic classes used in the management of renal conditions and describe their mechanisms of action.
Describe the indications, contraindications, adverse effects, and clinically significant interactions associated with medications used to treat renal conditions.
Compare pharmacologic agents within and across therapeutic classes to distinguish clinically relevant differences in efficacy, safety, and use.
Select appropriate pharmacologic therapy for common renal conditions based on clinical presentation and patient-specific factors.
Identify appropriate dosing, administration, and monitoring considerations for medications used in renal conditions.
Explain important medication-use and safety information to patients receiving pharmacotherapy for renal.
Describe the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and identify where each antihypertensive drug class acts.
Explain why ACE inhibitors and ARBs are preferred first-line therapy for hypertension in chronic kidney disease, including their renoprotective mechanism.
Identify major antihypertensive drug classes beyond RAAS blockers, their mechanisms, and their role in CKD-specific management.
Describe vasodilator pharmacology (nitrates, calcium channel blockers) in angina pectoris and its mechanistic overlap with cardiovascular-renal disease management.

Identify high-risk drug combinations and monitoring needs at the cardiorenal interface, including the "triple whammy," and apply the full renal/cardiorenal toolkit to integrated clinical scenarios with a cumulative recall quiz.

about.text: **PA PHARMACOLOGY COURSE · LECTURE 5 · SESSION 2 OF 2** — Renal Pharmacotherapeutics. **Session 2: Hypertension in CKD and the Cardiovascular-Renal Overlap  |  Thursday, November 19  |  8:30–11:00 AM**

Recap: Session 1 covered renal dosing principles and the five diuretic classes, organized by nephron site — Session 1 gave us nephron sites — plus the hyperkalemia-with-ACEi/ARB preview from the closing case.

Today we follow one pathway, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, then see where it intersects with angina drugs and with the most preventable cause of AKI, the triple whammy — closing with a cumulative recall quiz spanning both sessions.

Appendix 1 abbreviation key: PO = by mouth; IV = intravenous; SL = sublingual; BID / TID / QID = two / three / four times daily; ER / SR = extended-release / sustained-release; IR = immediate-release; HF = heart failure; MI = myocardial infarction.

LV = left ventricular; EF = ejection fraction; AV = atrioventricular; SVT = supraventricular tachycardia; WPW = Wolff-Parkinson-White; CAD = coronary artery disease; ECG = electrocardiogram; ICP = intracranial pressure; CBC = complete blood count.

ACE = angiotensin-converting enzyme; ARB = angiotensin receptor blocker; AKI = acute kidney injury; CKD = chronic kidney disease; CrCl = creatinine clearance; eGFR = estimated glomerular filtration rate; PDE5 = phosphodiesterase type 5; CYP = cytochrome P450.

The profiles give **Formulation, dose, indications, adverse effects, contraindications and toxicity** — your study reference: know the dose logic, the serious adverse effects, the contraindication that changes decisions and the toxicity you would need to recognize. **Standard adult dosing for teaching; verify against current prescribing information.**
**Appendix 2: DRUG PROFILE · SUPPORTING** — supporting drugs explain interactions, not doses. **Listed for context; not profiled in detail.**

**Original figures in this deck:** Figures 8, 12, 15, 16 and 18 (The Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System: Where Antihypertensives Act; Antihypertensive Classes: BP-Lowering Efficacy vs. Renoprotection in CKD; Angina Pathophysiology: Where Nitrates and Calcium Channel Blockers Act;

The "Triple Whammy": A Classic Preventable Cause of AKI; The Cardiorenal-Hypertension Cycle) were generated by the course director using the AI tool Claude to illustrate standard, non-copyrighted pharmacologic concepts — original diagrams, not reproduced from Katzung’s Basic and Clinical Pharmacology or any other copyrighted source.

**Mechanism illustrations:** Figures 9, 10, 11, 13, 14 and 17 are illustrative AI-generated schematics of drug mechanisms, not reproduced from any copyrighted source. **Reference:** Anthropic. (2026). Claude (Sonnet 5) [Large language model]. https://claude.ai

overview.text: **One pathway, four drug classes, and the preferred therapy for hypertension in CKD.** Today we follow the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, the pathway these drugs act on.

**Figure 8. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): angiotensinogen is converted to angiotensin I by renin, then to angiotensin II by ACE; angiotensin II drives both vasoconstriction and aldosterone release.**
**Direct renin inhibitors, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and aldosterone antagonists each block a different point in this cascade.**
This is the conceptual spine for the session: walk the cascade before naming drugs — angiotensinogen, renin, angiotensin I, ACE, angiotensin II, vasoconstriction and aldosterone.

prototype.text: ACE inhibitors: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril — "-pril" suffix across the class. ARBs: losartan, valsartan — "-sartan" suffix. Direct renin inhibitor: aliskiren.

moa.text: **Mechanism: block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, reducing both vasoconstriction and aldosterone release (Figure 8).**

ACE also breaks down bradykinin: ACE inhibitor blocks ACE → less angiotensin II (less vasoconstriction and aldosterone) → less bradykinin breakdown, so bradykinin accumulates → cough or angioedema → switch to an ARB for cough.
ARBs block the AT1 receptor directly, rather than preventing angiotensin II formation. Aliskiren blocks the rate-limiting first step of the entire cascade.

Renoprotection: by reducing angiotensin II, these drugs preferentially dilate the efferent (outflow) arteriole of the glomerulus, lowering intraglomerular pressure and reducing proteinuria — a direct, structural renoprotective effect beyond systemic BP control.

Chain (Figure 10): angiotensin II normally constricts the efferent arteriole → ACE inhibitor or ARB removes that signal → efferent arteriole dilates; intraglomerular pressure falls → proteinuria falls; creatinine rises up to ~30%.

indications.text: **ACE inhibitors and ARBs are first-line antihypertensive therapy in CKD, especially with proteinuria — not simply because they lower blood pressure.**
ARBs: no bradykinin-related cough — preferred alternative when ACE inhibitor cough is intolerable. ARBs do not raise bradykinin, so they are the usual switch.
Aliskiren: limited clinical use; useful mainly as a teaching example of where a drug could act upstream of ACE — included for conceptual completeness on Figure 8.
The drug class students might expect to avoid in kidney disease is actually the preferred therapy, precisely because of how it works at the glomerulus.

adverse.text: **Adverse effects: dry cough (bradykinin accumulation — the single most common reason for switching to an ARB), angioedema (rare but potentially life-threatening), and hyperkalemia.**
Cough is bradykinin-mediated, not allergic. Angioedema is rare but can be life-threatening: stop the drug.

An initial rise in serum creatinine of up to ~30% after starting therapy is expected and acceptable — reflects reduced intraglomerular pressure, not drug-induced kidney injury; a larger rise warrants evaluation for renal artery stenosis.

Students frequently get the creatinine point wrong: many want to stop the ACE inhibitor at the first rise. It is a predictable hemodynamic effect, not toxicity — the mechanism and the "side effect" are two faces of the same action.

contra.text: **Contraindicated in pregnancy — fetal renal toxicity; avoid in women who are or may become pregnant.** ARBs share the same pregnancy contraindication and hyperkalemia risk as ACE inhibitors.
Aliskiren: generally not combined with an ACE inhibitor or ARB due to additive hyperkalemia/hypotension risk with no added benefit — never in diabetes.

interactions.text: Potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics and trimethoprim: hyperkalemia with ACE inhibitors and ARBs. NSAIDs blunt antihypertensives and raise AKI risk with an ACE inhibitor or ARB plus diuretic.
Hyperkalemia with potassium-sparing diuretics rises with drugs that cut renin or angiotensin II: β blockers, NSAIDs, aliskiren, ACE inhibitors, ARBs.

pk.text: Enalapril’s ACE-inhibition half-life is about 4 hours, yet once-daily dosing works: concentrations stay far above the C50, so ACE stays inhibited.

monitoring.text: **Monitor potassium and renal function within 1–2 weeks of starting or up-titrating therapy, and periodically thereafter.**
**Hold or use with caution during acute illness causing volume depletion ("sick day rules") — combined with reduced renal perfusion, RAAS blockade can precipitate acute kidney injury.**

Sick-day rules: hold the ACE inhibitor or ARB during vomiting, diarrhea or dehydration. An early creatinine rise is expected and hemodynamic, not nephrotoxicity; a larger rise warrants checking for volume depletion or renal artery stenosis.

pearls.text: Case: a patient with hypertension and diabetic nephropathy is started on lisinopril; two weeks later serum creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 1.4 mg/dL. **Is this an indication to stop the ACE inhibitor?**
**A rise of roughly 27% is within the expected range for ACE inhibitor initiation, reflecting reduced intraglomerular pressure from efferent arteriolar dilation — not drug toxicity.**
**Therapy should generally continue with ongoing monitoring; a rise beyond approximately 30%, or a much sharper increase, should prompt evaluation for renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.**
A student who reflexively says "stop the drug" has missed that this creatinine rise is expected and even reflects the mechanism working as intended.

hooks.text: Why does creatinine rise on an ACE inhibitor? The drug lowers glomerular pressure on purpose — that same drop protects the kidney from proteinuria.
Thirty is fine, more is a sign: up to ~30% creatinine rise → continue; more → look for renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.

high_yield.text: ACEi/ARB first-line in proteinuric CKD: efferent dilation lowers intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria.
Creatinine rise up to ~30% is expected; check K⁺ and creatinine in 1–2 weeks; sick-day rules; never in pregnancy.

overview.text: **RAAS blockers are first-line — but rarely the whole story.** Other major classes: CCBs, beta-blockers, diuretics, central agents and direct vasodilators.
This four-card slide is a brief classification recap — CCBs and beta-blockers get fuller treatment later this session (angina) and in cardiovascular coursework.

prototype.text: Calcium channel blockers: dihydropyridines (amlodipine) and non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil). Beta-blockers: metoprolol, atenolol. Central α2 agonists: clonidine, methyldopa. Direct arteriolar vasodilator: hydralazine.

moa.text: Dihydropyridines (amlodipine): arteriolar dilation. Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil): also ↓ HR/contractility.
Beta-blockers: ↓ heart rate, ↓ contractility, ↓ renin release.
Chain (Figure 11): dihydropyridine arteriolar dilation → afterload falls; blood pressure lowers. Non-DHP CCB or beta-blocker: heart rate and contractility fall → renin release falls.
Clonidine or methyldopa stimulates central α2 receptors → sympathetic outflow falls, so BP falls. Hydralazine dilates arterioles directly → reflex tachycardia and fluid retention.

indications.text: Beta-blockers: not generally first-line for uncomplicated HTN, but compelling indications include concurrent CAD/heart failure/arrhythmia.

If all these classes lower blood pressure similarly, why are RAAS blockers preferred in CKD? Similar BP lowering; ACE inhibitors and ARBs add renoprotection — the renoprotective gap in Figure 12, not a difference in BP control.
Thiazide / loop diuretics (covered in depth in Session 1): thiazides first-line with preserved renal function; loops preferred as GFR falls.
Central agents (clonidine, methyldopa) and hydralazine: reserved for resistant hypertension or specific situations (e.g., methyldopa in pregnancy).
Diuretics enhance the efficacy of many agents, particularly ACE inhibitors; hydralazine and minoxidil need a diuretic because they cause salt and water retention.
Spironolactone may be the most effective single agent for drug-resistant hypertension.

adverse.text: Peripheral edema is a CCB class adverse effect.
Hydralazine: reflex tachycardia and fluid retention — must be paired with a beta-blocker and a diuretic.
Abrupt clonidine withdrawal causes rebound hypertension.

contra.text: Atenolol accumulates in renal impairment (reduce dose when CrCl is below 35 mL/min); beta-blockers: do not stop abruptly.

interactions.text: Diltiazem or verapamil with a beta-blocker risks bradycardia and AV block; dihydropyridines pair with beta-blockers without that conduction risk.
Verapamil and diltiazem raise digoxin levels. Rifampin and carbamazepine lower CCB levels; grapefruit juice raises dihydropyridine levels.

monitoring.text: **Resistant hypertension (BP above goal despite three or more antihypertensive classes, including a diuretic) is common in CKD, often driven by volume overload.**
First step: confirm diuretic therapy is adequate — a thiazide may simply no longer be effective at the patient’s current GFR (Session 1’s loop-vs-thiazide cutoff).
Switching from a thiazide to a loop diuretic, or increasing loop diuretic dosing, is often the most effective single change in advanced CKD.
**Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) can be added for resistant hypertension, but require close potassium and renal-function monitoring, especially on top of an ACE inhibitor or ARB.**

pearls.text: "Resistant hypertension in CKD" is often really a diuretic-selection problem, not a need for an entirely new drug class — check diuretic adequacy first; thiazide to loop switch; add spironolactone with close monitoring.

Case: CKD (eGFR 28 mL/min), still hypertensive despite lisinopril, amlodipine, and hydrochlorothiazide. **What is the most likely contributor to inadequate control, and what change would you suggest first?**

**At this GFR, hydrochlorothiazide has largely lost its natriuretic efficacy (Session 1). Switching to a loop diuretic such as furosemide or torsemide is usually the most effective next step before adding an entirely new drug class.**
This case is a direct callback to the Session 1 "Choosing a Diuretic for Advancing CKD" case — point out the parallel if you remember it.

figures.caption: **Schematic (illustrative)** — Figure 11. Vascular versus cardiac targets of antihypertensive drugs: dihydropyridines dilate arterioles (afterload falls); non-dihydropyridines and beta-blockers slow heart rate and contractility (beta-blockers also cut renin).

viz.title: CCBs and beta-blockers: different targets
viz.point: Vessel drugs vs. heart drugs — never stack two heart-slowers.

drugs.label: Diltiazem / verapamil
drugs.note: ↓ HR and contractility; avoid with beta-blockers (AV block) (S13).

overview.text: **Where cardiovascular and renal pharmacology converge — and where that convergence can go wrong.** This section covers vasodilators and angina, then the cardiorenal overlap.
**Figure 15. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): angina results when myocardial oxygen demand exceeds supply; nitrates reduce preload, dihydropyridine CCBs reduce afterload,**
**non-dihydropyridine CCBs also reduce heart rate/contractility and increase coronary flow, and beta-blockers reduce heart rate and contractility.**
This figure organizes every antianginal drug class by exactly which side of the supply/demand equation it affects — sort nitrates, each CCB subtype, and beta-blockers onto it from memory.

prototype.text: Nitroglycerin (sublingual for acute angina; IV/patch for sustained use), isosorbide mononitrate/dinitrate (oral, longer-acting).

moa.text: **Mechanism: release nitric oxide, activating guanylate cyclase and increasing cGMP, producing smooth muscle relaxation — predominantly venodilation at usual doses, reducing preload and myocardial oxygen demand.**
Chain (Figure 14): nitrate donates nitric oxide (NO) → NO activates guanylate cyclase, so cGMP rises → cGMP relaxes smooth muscle: venodilation → preload and oxygen demand fall.
**Dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine) — predominantly arteriolar dilation, reducing afterload; the same mechanism used for hypertension (Section 5).**

**Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil) — also reduce heart rate and contractility and increase coronary blood flow; avoid combining with beta-blockers due to additive bradycardia/AV block risk.**

indications.text: CCBs are the clearest example in the unit of the same drug class, same mechanism, treating two different conditions (hypertension and angina).

This is the deliberate cardiovascular-renal "overlap" moment the lecture title promises — calcium channel blockers are not a separate topic from the antihypertensive content in Section 5; they are the same drugs doing double duty.

adverse.text: **Adverse effects: headache (vasodilation), reflex tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension.**
**Adverse effects: peripheral edema and reflex tachycardia (dihydropyridines); bradycardia, AV block, and constipation (non-dihydropyridines, especially verapamil).**

contra.text: **Absolute contraindication: concurrent use with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil and similar) — the combination can cause life-threatening hypotension.**
PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenafil block cGMP breakdown, causing severe hypotension with nitrates.
The PDE5-inhibitor interaction is one of the highest-stakes medication-safety points in this whole unit — a real-world, repeatedly tested safety question worth a memorable callout.

interactions.text: **Figure 16. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): an NSAID (afferent arteriolar constriction), an ACE inhibitor or ARB (efferent arteriolar dilation), and a diuretic (volume depletion) each independently reduce glomerular filtration pressure —**
**combined, the effect on kidney perfusion is additive to synergistic, substantially raising acute kidney injury risk.** An extremely common, often missed, entirely preventable cause of AKI.
Three hits (Figure 17): NSAID constricts the afferent arteriole → ACE inhibitor or ARB dilates the efferent arteriole → diuretic causes volume depletion → filtration pressure collapses: AKI.
NSAIDs blunt loop and thiazide action by reducing renal prostaglandins — significant in nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis.

monitoring.text: Tolerance develops with continuous exposure — a nitrate-free interval (typically overnight) is required to maintain efficacy with long-acting formulations.
Prevention: counsel patients about over-the-counter NSAIDs — ask which OTC NSAIDs they commonly take.

pearls.text: The triple whammy is the capstone cardiorenal interaction: Session 1’s diuretics + this session’s RAAS blockers + NSAIDs students will meet constantly in practice.
Hypertension → CKD: uncontrolled blood pressure causes glomerular capillary injury and nephrosclerosis over time — a leading cause of CKD progression, alongside diabetes.
CKD → hypertension: reduced renal function causes volume overload and RAAS activation, which worsens and complicates blood pressure control, often requiring multiple drug classes.

**Figure 18. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): hypertension and chronic kidney disease drive one another in a self-reinforcing cycle — uncontrolled blood pressure causes glomerular injury and CKD progression,**
**while CKD causes volume overload and RAAS activation that worsens hypertension.**
Figure 18 is the conceptual closer for the whole unit — tie it back to Figure 8: RAAS blockade is effective precisely because it intervenes in both directions of this cycle at once.

Case: an older adult on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide starts a regular OTC NSAID for a knee injury; one week later, lethargy and an acute rise in creatinine. **What is the most likely explanation, and how could this have been prevented?**

**This is a classic "triple whammy" presentation (Figure 16) — the NSAID, ACE inhibitor, and diuretic each independently reduced glomerular filtration pressure, and together precipitated acute kidney injury.**
**Prevention requires counseling patients on RAAS blockers and diuretics to avoid regular NSAID use and to seek guidance before starting one, even an over-the-counter product.**
This case is the direct clinical application of Figure 16 and reinforces IO5.6 (patient counseling): the preventable element is entirely what the patient was or wasn’t told about OTC NSAID use.

Same patient, eGFR now 25: hydrochlorothiazide has likely lost much of its efficacy — switching to a loop diuretic (furosemide, torsemide) is more effective for blood pressure regardless of the NSAID issue.
Counsel the patient to avoid regular OTC NSAID use and to check with a prescriber or pharmacist before starting any new OTC product, given the RAAS blocker + diuretic combination already in place.

classes.name: Putting It All Together: Renal Toolkit

definitions.text: **Applying the whole Renal pharmacology toolkit.** Integration: put the drug classes together — for each patient, name a first-line approach AND the single biggest safety concern to check before prescribing or counseling.

how.text: **1.** Diuretic classes (Session 1) and RAAS-blocking antihypertensives both map onto specific, drug-targetable points in renal physiology — the nephron (Figure 1) and the RAAS cascade (Figure 8), respectively.
**2.** ACE inhibitors and ARBs are preferred first-line therapy for hypertension in CKD because of their renoprotective efferent-arteriolar mechanism, not just their blood-pressure-lowering effect.
**3.** Calcium channel blockers exemplify the cardiovascular-renal overlap directly — the same drug class, same mechanism, treats both hypertension and angina.
**4.** The "triple whammy" (NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic) is a classic, common, and preventable cause of acute kidney injury that draws on content from both sessions at once.
**5.** Hypertension and chronic kidney disease exist in a bidirectional, self-reinforcing cycle (Figure 18) — which is exactly why managing one well so often means managing the other.
All three threads center on glomerular filtration pressure.

Connecting back to earlier units: drug-metabolism/dosing concepts (Unit 1) and the biologic-mechanism callbacks from Units 2–4 all reinforce that pharmacology is cumulative — the cardiorenal interface is where several organ-system units visibly intersect.

clinical.text: **Patient A — advancing CKD, hypertension no longer controlled on a thiazide:** switch to a loop diuretic; check potassium and volume status.
**Patient B — proteinuric CKD, needs first-line antihypertensive therapy:** ACE inhibitor or ARB; check potassium and creatinine in 1–2 weeks and pregnancy potential.
**Patient C — on an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic, about to start a daily OTC NSAID:** counsel against regular NSAID use — triple whammy AKI risk.

**Patient D — stable angina, already on a beta-blocker, needs additional symptom control:** add a dihydropyridine CCB or a long-acting nitrate; avoid diltiazem/verapamil (AV block) and PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates.

examples.text: **A cumulative self-test spanning both sessions — use this to review before exams.** The recall quiz is a standalone resource, separate from in-lecture quick checks.
**Recall Q1–2:** loops collapse the lumen-positive potential (↑ Ca²⁺ excretion), thiazides increase distal Ca²⁺ reabsorption; at eGFR 22 switch the thiazide to a loop.
**Recall Q3–4:** a creatinine rise up to ~30% on an ACE inhibitor is expected — continue with monitoring; ACEi/ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria.
**Recall Q5:** the triple whammy is three independent reductions in filtration pressure combining additively to synergistically, precipitating AKI.

**Recall Q6:** CCBs treat hypertension via arteriolar dilation (reducing afterload/systemic vascular resistance) and angina via the same mechanism (reducing afterload and myocardial oxygen demand) — one drug class, one mechanism, two indications.

traps.text: Reflexively stopping an ACE inhibitor for a ≤30% creatinine rise is the classic trap.
Adding a new drug class when the real problem is a thiazide at low GFR.

summary.text: The **RAAS**: angiotensinogen → (renin) → angiotensin I → (ACE) → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone; aliskiren, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and aldosterone antagonists each block one step.

**ACE inhibitors/ARBs** are first-line in proteinuric CKD: efferent dilation lowers glomerular pressure; a creatinine rise **up to ~30%** is expected; check K⁺/creatinine in 1–2 weeks; **never in pregnancy**.

summary.text: ACE-inhibitor **cough** is bradykinin, not allergy → switch to an **ARB**; angioedema → stop.
**Non-DHP CCBs + beta-blockers** → bradycardia/AV block; resistant HTN in CKD is often a thiazide that needs to become a **loop**.
**Nitrates**: NO → cGMP → venodilation; nitrate-free interval; **never with PDE5 inhibitors**. **CCBs** treat both hypertension and angina by the same mechanism.
**Triple whammy**: NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic → AKI; counsel against OTC NSAIDs.
